title: Forgiveness: pardon and overlook
hook: a father swears to cut off the relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him a question

segments.voice: Yesterday: sidq, truthfulness, and the company of the truthful. Today, what to do when someone close has not been truthful at all, a story day four hundred ninety-six first told.

Abu Bakr had been supporting a poor relative, a man named Mistah. Then a false accusation spread through Medina about Abu Bakr's own daughter, 'A'ishah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. And Mistah was one of those who repeated it. When the Qur'an cleared her name, Abu Bakr made an oath, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: by Allah, I will never spend anything on Mistah again. On its face, a fair oath. A verse came down about it anyway.
screen: `ABU BAKR SUPPORTED MISTAH.` → `MISTAH SPREAD THE SLANDER.` → `AN OATH: NEVER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The verse is in surah al-Nur. It speaks to people of means who swear off giving to their relatives and the needy. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." Two verbs, in Arabic wal-ya'fu wal-yasfahu: pardon, and overlook. 'Afw is letting go of what you're owed: the debt, the punishment, the right to get even. Overlooking goes one step further: not raising it again, not keeping it ready for the next argument. Then the question. The verse doesn't argue that Mistah deserved help, or that the slander was small. It asks Abu Bakr about himself: do you want to be forgiven? His answer, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me. And he went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Notice the order. The wrong was named first; 'A'ishah's innocence was declared in the Qur'an itself. Pardon came after the truth, not instead of it. The hadith from the humility day, in Sahih Muslim, has a line for this too, in paraphrase: no servant pardons except that Allah increases him in honor. So 'afw isn't pretending. It's choosing, with the wrong fully seen, to let the debt go, and then to stop bringing it up.
screen: `AL-NUR: FORGIVE AND SHOW INDULGENCE.` · `PARDON, THEN OVERLOOK.` · `DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `THE TRUTH FIRST, THEN PARDON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who owes you something, an apology, money, a fairer word: not the deepest wound you carry, just something you can hold, and name the wrong plainly without shrinking it. Then hear the verse's question turned toward you, is there anything you hope to be forgiven for, and if you're ready, let one piece of the debt go, maybe not all of it. If you pray, you can say the verse's last words in your heart: Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
'Afw. Pardon: letting go of what you're owed, with the wrong fully seen, and then overlooking it, not bringing it up again. Today's word.
Your line: pardon and overlook. The truth first, then the letting go. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Islamic teaching on pardon draws on Qur'an 24:22 and the story of Abu Bakr resuming his support for Mistah, and on the hadith that Allah increases in honor a servant who pardons.
